name: Heliotrope
lede: Heliotrope is a purple named for a flowering shrub, famous in late Victorian fashion for its bright combinations, its place in mourning dress and its appearance on stage in Oscar Wilde.

sections.title: A plant that follows the sun
sections.body:
The shrub's name joins two Greek words, *helios* for the sun and *tropaios* for turning, because the purple flowers were said to follow the sun across the sky [1]. St Clair notes that the shrub follows light no more than other plants do, and that what sets it apart is its sweet scent, which he likens to cherry pie [1]. A distant ancestor of the plant went into perfume in ancient Egypt and was traded with Greece and Rome [1].

The color is named for the blooms [1]. The dictionary files heliotrope with the purples, and lists several related shades, among them heliotrope grey [2].

sections.title: The Victorian vogue
sections.body:
The color's high point came late in the nineteenth century, a boom time for purples [1]. Part of the appeal was novelty: before Perkin's [[mauve]], purple had been hard to make, and it kept the glamour of ancient imperial status [1]. Fashion writers paired heliotrope in 1880 with light green or apricot, and later with shades as varied as canary yellow, eucalyptus green, bronze and peacock blue [1]. One commentator remarked that no colors seemed too bright and the combinations were sometimes startling [1].

In the Victorian language of flowers heliotrope often meant devotion [1]. That is partly why it was among the few colors women could wear after a bereavement [1]. Heliotrope and other soft purples belonged to half-mourning, which for a widow began only after two years of plain, matte black [1]. After a serious influenza outbreak in the winter of 1890, black, grey and heliotrope were worn in profusion the next year [1].

On the page, the color marks a character. Mrs Cheveley, the immoral heroine of Wilde's *An Ideal Husband*, enters wearing heliotrope and diamonds [1]. St Clair adds that allusions to it appear in the work of Rowling, D. H. Lawrence, Wodehouse, Joyce and Conrad [1].

sections.title: The swatch and the shade
sections.body: The screen swatch is a vivid orchid-violet, far brighter than the softer purples that half-mourning allowed. The books do not give the Victorian shade as a numeric color, so the match is a matter of eye and not of data [3]. A grey-toned neighbor in the names data, Dark Heliotrope Grey, shows how muted some shades with the name were [3]. Look to [[lilac]], [[violet]] and [[orchid]] for related colors in this range [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
The swatch measures a lightness of 66 and a chroma of about 82, with a hue angle of 320 degrees, so it lies between violet and magenta [3]. Its contrast ratio against white is only 2.6 to 1 [3]. The nearest named colors in the data are Easter Purple at about 10 units and Ultra Pink at about 12 [3].

We have not computed how often this swatch occurs in paintings, so we make no claim about the archive. Screen colors are approximate [3].
